Rid
rid
v. (to free, to deliver out of the hand of another; to clear away)
Old Norse rydja, to clear. In the Authorized Version rid is a rescue word: to rid a man is to get him out of somebody's hand, and the phrase that follows it is nearly always out of the hand of.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The word's great occurrence is in the second of the four great I wills of the exodus: “I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments” (Exo 6:6). Bring out, rid, redeem — three stages of one deliverance, and every verb has God for its subject. The passover cups of the Jewish seder were built on these promises. Reuben uses the word for a rescue he intended and did not carry out: “Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit… that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again” (Gen 37:22). Reuben meant well, acted by half measures, and came back to an empty pit. Good intentions that avoid confrontation usually arrive too late. Psalm 82 makes it a command to judges: “Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked” (Psa 82:4) — the magistrate's office is defined by whose hand he takes people out of. David prays it for himself twice in one psalm: “Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters” (Psa 144:7). And Leviticus promises it of the land itself: “I will rid evil beasts out of the land” (Lev 26:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rid as to free, to deliver; to set free, to release; and to drive away, to remove by violence.

expand to see more

RID, v.t. To free; to deliver; as, to rid one from his troubles.

1. To separate; to drive away.

2. To free; to clear; to disencumber; as, to rid the house of vermin.

3. To dispatch. I will rid you out of their bondage. Exodus 6.

RIDDANCE, n. Deliverance; a setting free.

Key Scripture

Exo 6:6 — "Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:"

Psa 82:4 — "Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."

Gen 37:22 — "And Reuben said unto them, Shed no blood, but cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, and lay no hand upon him; that he might rid him out of their hands, to deliver him to his father again."

Psa 144:7 — "Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children;"

Modern Corruption

Deliverance is described as self-liberation; every biblical use of this verb puts the rescue in another's hand.

expand to see more

The governing story of the age is self-liberation: a person frees himself, throws off what binds him, and becomes what he chooses. Every occurrence of this verb in Scripture describes the opposite grammar. I will bring you out… I will rid you… I will redeem you — four times God is the subject and Israel is the object, and Israel's contribution to the exodus was to be too weak to leave. The gospel keeps the same structure: men are delivered from the power of darkness and translated into the kingdom of God's dear Son, and the verbs belong to God.

Reuben is the cautionary figure, and he is more familiar than we like. He genuinely intended to save Joseph, he opposed the murder, and he arranged a half measure that would let him rescue the boy later without confronting his brothers now. He came back and the pit was empty, and he rent his clothes and said whither shall I go? Half measures to avoid confrontation are a common form of cowardice among decent men, and they characteristically produce grief rather than safety. Psalm 82 tells the man with authority to do the harder thing: rid them out of the hand of the wicked — which requires taking hold.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew natsal (H5337), to snatch away, to deliver; ga'al (H1350), to redeem as a kinsman; shabath (H7673), to cause to cease.

expand to see more

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to strip away, to snatch out of the hand of, to deliver; Exodus 6:6, Psalm 82:4, 144:7, 144:11.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to act as kinsman, to redeem; the third verb of Exodus 6:6, I will redeem you.

Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, to cause to cease; Leviticus 26:6, I will rid evil beasts out of the land.

Hebrew yad (H3027) — hand; the standing idiom — delivered out of the hand of.

Greek rhuomai (G4506) — to draw to oneself, to rescue; Matthew 6:13, deliver us from evil; Colossians 1:13.

Usage

"“I will rid you out of their bondage” — the second of the four I wills."

"“Rid them out of the hand of the wicked” — the magistrate's office defined."

"“That he might rid him out of their hands” — and Reuben came back to an empty pit."
